name: Clabber
description: Clabber is a trick-taking card game of the Jass/Belote family, uniquely popular in Evansville, Indiana and surrounding areas. It is played with a 24-card deck (Ac-9) and features complex trump rankings and a 'meld' system where card combinations like 'Dad' (3-card sequence) and 'Mule' (4 Jacks) score bonus points. The game is highly strategic, requiring players to choose trumps carefully and compete for the prestigious 'last trick' bonus. It is colloquially known as 'Dad' after its most common sequence meld.
deck: 24 cards (A, K, Q, J, 10, 9 of each suit)

history.origins: Brought to Indiana by German and Central European immigrants, Clabber is a local evolution of the European Klabberjass. It became a cultural staple in Evansville, often played in taverns and social clubs.
timeline: 19th Century: European Klabberjass variants arrive in the American Midwest.
Early 20th Century: The game stabilizes into the 'Clabber' format in Evansville, Indiana.
Modern: Still actively played in local tournaments and social gatherings, featuring distinctive 'special' score sheets.
history.cultural: In Evansville, Clabber is more than a game; it's a regional identity. The scoring 'XX' (turkey tracks) and the specific local vernacular distinguish it from generic Jass variants.
history.evolution: The game retains the 'Bela' (Bell) and 'Darda' (Dad) terminology from its Jass ancestry but has specialized local scoring rules and jargon like 'Mule' for four Jacks.

setup.players: 4 players in fixed partnerships (North-South vs East-West).
setup.dealing: Dealer deals all 24 cards one at a time clockwise; each player receives six cards. The last card (dealer's) is turned face up; its suit is the trump candidate for the first round of bidding.
setup.equipment: 24 cards and a 'Clabber' score sheet (typically with 4 columns for tracking team scores and addition-checks).

rules.objective: Be the first team to reach 500 points by winning tricks with high-value cards and declaring melds.
rules.gameplay: Must follow suit. If void in the led suit, you MUST play a trump. If trumps are led, you MUST 'overtrump' (play a higher trump) if able. The last trick scores a 10-point bonus.
keyRules: No card can be used in more than one meld (except Bell cards).
Meld must be announced during the first trick and shown before the second.
Trump-maker must have at least one card of the named suit to 'play'.
Turkey Tracks: An 'XX' on the score sheet when a team is set.

strategy.basic: Prioritize winning the Jack and Nine of trumps (The 'Jass' and 'Manille' equivalents). Count the 24 cards carefully to identify when it is safe to lead point-heavy cards like Aces and Tens.
strategy.intermediate: Use your 'Dad' or 'Fifty' sequences to force opponents into a set. Manage your trumps to ensure you win the last trick (10 pts) and secure the win.
strategy.advanced: Defensive play: If you are the opponents, focus on 'hicking' the bidders by forcing them to use their high trumps on low-value tricks, then taking the point-heavy late cards.
tips: Announce your Bell (K-Q) when playing the second card to ensure the 20 points.
Don't lead a lone non-trump Ace if trumps haven't been cleared; it's a prime target for a ruff.
The 'Mule' (4 Jacks) is almost an automatic round win - protect those Jacks at all costs.

scoring.description: Cumulative score to 500. Points come from card values in tricks (J=20, 9=14 in trumps), melds, and the last trick bonus.
scoring.winCondition: The first team to reach or exceed 500 points wins.

synthesis.shortDescription: Evansville's favorite trick-taking game. Use a 24-card deck, declare 'Dads' and 'Mules' for points, and watch out for the 'Turkey Tracks' if your team gets hicked.
